questions.question: Q: What is the age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales?

points.text: The age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales is 10. This means children aged 10 and over can be arrested, charged, and prosecuted for criminal offences. Critics argue this is too low compared to other European countries where it is typically 14.

questions.question: Q: How does the youth justice system differ from the adult system?

points.text: Youth courts are less formal with no public gallery and no wigs. Parents or guardians must attend. Sentences focus on rehabilitation rather than punishment, with options like Referral Orders and Youth Rehabilitation Orders instead of prison for most offences. Reporting restrictions protect the young person's identity.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate whether the age of criminal responsibility should be raised.

points.text: Arguments for raising: 10-year-olds may not fully understand the consequences of their actions; other European countries set it at 14 or higher; it could prevent criminalising vulnerable children who need support not punishment. Arguments against: serious offences still need consequences; victims deserve justice; a lower age allows early intervention through the youth justice system.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: The youth justice system attempts to prioritise rehabilitation over punishment, reflecting that young people may not fully understand the consequences of their actions. Youth courts use less formal procedures, and sentences such as Referral Orders and Youth Rehabilitation Orders focus on addressing the causes of offending rather than simply punishing. Multi-agency youth offending teams work with families and communities to prevent reoffending. This approach has had some success. Youth offending rates have fallen significantly since 2007, suggesting rehabilitation-focused interventions can work. Referral Orders have relatively high completion rates and victim satisfaction. However, the system is not wholly rehabilitative. The age of criminal responsibility at 10 is one of the lowest in Europe, meaning very young children can be drawn into the criminal justice system. Custodial sentences are still available and used for serious offences, and conditions in Young Offender Institutions have been criticised. Reoffending rates remain high at around 40% within 12 months. Overall, while the youth justice system has a stronger rehabilitative focus than the adult system, the persistence of a low criminal responsibility age and high reoffending rates suggest it does not yet fully achieve the balance it aims for.
